name: Online Services
description: Iran’s online services include platforms for requesting transport, finding goods and services, and arranging everyday tasks. Ride-hailing platforms and classified-advertising services illustrate different ways digital interfaces connect users with people and businesses.

seo.title: Online Services in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Understand Iran’s online service platforms, from ride-hailing to classified advertising, and the differences between their business models.

content.heading: Different platforms solve different problems
content.content:
An online service is best understood by examining what happens after a user opens the interface. Tapsi describes its core offering as an online platform for requesting rides and couriers. Sheypoor presents a classified-advertising directory covering vehicles, property, employment, services, and consumer goods. These are different activities: requesting transport initiates a service request, while browsing an advertisement begins the search for a suitable seller, employer, property, or provider. [s1][s2]

This distinction helps international readers navigate the sector. A transport platform should be examined through the journey it coordinates; a classified service through the information it makes discoverable. An advertisement, a booking, and a completed service are separate events. Their volumes should not be added together as if they measured the same economic activity. This is an editorial framework for comparing the platforms, rather than a claim that they share one operating model. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Classified advertising and access through the web
content.content:
Sheypoor’s categories show how broadly a classified service can extend beyond second-hand household goods. Its inspected homepage includes employment, business services, industrial and commercial equipment, electronics, property, and vehicles. A single directory can therefore serve several distinct purposes: finding work, advertising professional services, locating equipment, or searching for a home. The existence of a category establishes the platform’s advertised scope; it does not establish the number or quality of transactions completed through it. [s2]

The interface also matters. Divar’s website explains access through a progressive web app, or PWA: a website that users can add to a phone’s home screen. Its instructions describe this option for both iOS and Android, without requiring a separate application download or manual app update. This provides a concrete example of how an Iranian platform offers access outside a conventional app-store installation. It does not establish that every feature works identically across devices. [s3]

content.heading: Connectivity is part of service infrastructure
content.content:
Online services depend on more than their own application code. Cloudflare’s analysis of Iran’s partial internet restoration in May 2026 describes substantial interruptions to international connectivity and an uneven recovery. Its measurements also distinguish traffic from the announcement of internet address space: a network can remain visible in routing information while users’ ability to exchange data is severely restricted. [s4]

For understanding a service platform, the implication is methodological. A reachable homepage is not proof that registration, maps, payments, notifications, or customer support work throughout the country. Conversely, international traffic measurements alone do not demonstrate that every domestic service has stopped. Platform availability needs evidence from the relevant service and location. The network research supports treating connectivity as a constraint, without assigning unmeasured outage losses to individual businesses. [s4]

content.heading: How to explore this branch
content.content:
The Snapp and Tapsi pages examine individual transport platforms. Divar and Sheypoor belong to the classified-advertising side of the directory, while the home-service and booking branches require separate research into how providers are selected, appointments are confirmed, and responsibility is divided between the platform and the service provider. These branch labels organize the guide; they are not evidence that every listed model has the same scale or contractual safeguards.

Useful comparisons should begin with precise questions: What does the platform undertake to arrange? Which part of the interaction remains between users? Does a reported number count accounts, requests, listings, or completed services? Answering those questions is more informative than treating all online activity as a single market. The inspected transport and classified pages support these distinctions, but do not provide a comprehensive measurement of Iran’s online-services economy. [s1][s2][s3]

name: Snapp
description: Snapp is an Iranian digital platform whose services extend from passenger transport to delivery, shopping, and travel. Its published reporting distinguishes the wider service ecosystem from Snapp Car, the passenger ride-hailing service. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Snapp: Transport and Everyday Services in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Snapp’s service ecosystem, reported passenger-trip activity, and the limits of company-published platform statistics.

content.heading: From transport to an everyday service interface
content.content:
Snapp’s company profile dates its establishment to 2014 and presents the business as a super app: an interface bringing several services together. Its description includes transport, delivery, food, groceries, and travel. The useful distinction is between Snapp as a shared consumer interface and the particular service fulfilling a request. A passenger journey and a grocery delivery belong to different operating activities even when accessed through the same application. [s2]

The group’s reporting for Solar Hijri year 1403 separately describes Snapp Car, Snapp Box, food delivery, grocery shopping, credit services, and travel booking. The names therefore should not be treated as interchangeable measures of one transport business. [s1]

content.heading: Reading the reported scale
content.content:
For Solar Hijri year 1403, Snapp reports passenger trips separately from registered and active accounts. Tehran had the largest reported city trip total, followed by Mashhad and Shiraz. Nationwide coverage consequently does not imply equal activity in every city. The annual trip observation below is a company-reported service count, not a count of unique people or all journeys made in Iran. [s1]

Account totals need similar care. An account registered at any point is different from an account active during a reporting year. Neither measure alone establishes how frequently a person travels, whether one person holds multiple accounts, or what share of household transport spending reaches the platform.

content.title: Company-reported Snapp Car trips: verified annual observation

content.heading: Safety functions and evidence of outcomes
content.content:
Namnak’s account of the group’s 1404 report describes facial reauthentication for drivers, masked calling, route-deviation detection, and an emergency-contact function. These are reported tools and procedures. Their presence does not independently establish how quickly assistance arrives or whether risk has declined. [s3]

The same distinction applies to environmental claims. Namnak attributes estimated emissions savings from shared trips to Snapp. Such estimates require a counterfactual: what journeys would otherwise have occurred, in which vehicles, and over what distances. Without the underlying method, a reported estimate should not become an independently verified statement of environmental benefit. [s3]

Snapp is consequently useful to study both as a service interface and as a producer of information about its own activity. Its reports document how it describes operations; independent evidence is still needed to evaluate worker conditions, consumer protection, and the effectiveness of safety systems.

name: Tapsi
description: Tapsi is an Iranian transport platform offering online ride-hailing and courier requests. Its company identity combines a consumer-facing transport brand with the legal company name Pishgaman Fanavari va Danesh Aramis. [s1][s3]

seo.title: Tapsi: Iran’s Ride-Hailing Platform | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: An evidence-based introduction to Tapsi’s transport services, company history, and the limits of available operating and financial data.

content.heading: A transport brand and a legal company
content.content:
Tapsi’s accessible English homepage identifies it as an online platform for requesting rides and couriers. Its corporate profile places its headquarters in Tehran and gives 2016 as its founding year. These sources support its basic identity as a technology-mediated transport business, without establishing that every advertised service is available in every city. [s1][s2]

Digiato distinguishes legal establishment from the start of operations. It identifies the company as Pishgaman Fanavari va Danesh Aramis, records establishment in Bahman 1394, and places the operational launch in Khordad 1395. These are Iranian Solar Hijri month-and-year labels; retaining them avoids inventing a precise Gregorian anniversary. Digiato names Milad Monshipour, Hamid Mahini, and Hooman Damirchi as founders. [s3]

content.heading: Passenger journeys and delivery requests
content.content:
Digiato’s company profile describes a service portfolio spanning standard passenger rides, a higher-specification ride option, shared journeys, motorcycle and car deliveries, and telephone requests. These descriptions help explain the brand’s transport focus, but they should be read as a documented portfolio rather than a verified live menu. Service names and availability can change, and the inspected profile does not establish availability by city and date. [s3]

The distinction between passenger transport and courier work matters when interpreting the business. Both involve matching a request to transport capacity, but their service outcomes differ: one moves a person, the other a consignment. A combined description of the platform does not make their operating statistics interchangeable. Tapsi’s own English heading explicitly identifies both activities. [s1]

content.heading: What the company says technology contributes
content.content:
In its corporate profile, Tapsi describes data analysis and deep-learning algorithms as tools for allocating transport resources. It also frames its ambitions around transport, environmental challenges, and employment. These statements establish the company’s stated approach and objectives. They do not independently demonstrate shorter waiting times, lower emissions, or better earnings for drivers. [s2]

Evaluating those outcomes would require evidence beyond a corporate description: consistent service measurements, a defined comparison, and an explanation of the population covered. The distinction is especially relevant when a platform’s public narrative combines a practical service with wider social benefits. The request interface can be documented directly; the claimed benefits require their own evidence.

content.heading: Why financial and operating measures need separate treatment
content.content:
Digiato reports that Tapsi entered the securities market and refers to financial disclosures on Codal, Iran’s issuer-disclosure system. The underlying filings were not inspected for this page, so the article’s financial figures are not reproduced as a verified annual dataset. [s3]

A fuller account should connect the consumer brand to dated issuer filings and distinguish company revenue from the value of passenger fares. It should also keep partial-year results separate from annual results and registered accounts separate from active passengers. Until comparable primary records are available, Tapsi can be described with confidence at the level of identity and advertised function, while its latest scale, ownership, and financial performance remain research tasks.
